title: Dancing Girl
altText: A playful painting of a pink, abstracted dancing figure with outstretched limbs, drawn in dark-brown lines and circles on a brown background. Small stick figures and touches of yellow, orange, green, pink and beige surround her.

context: Painted in 1940 by Paul Klee. The museum says that after the Nazis came to power Klee lost his teaching post in 1933 and went into exile in Switzerland, and that from 1937 to 1940 he regained momentum, producing many paintings and drawings. It also notes his humor: he made his signature by laying a monogrammed handkerchief over the surface.

descriptions.k: A pink dancer kicks up her arms and legs! Little stick people dance around her. The lines are dark and the background is brown. Can you strike her pose? Which small figure do you like?
descriptions.g12: Paul Klee painted a dancing girl in pink with arms and legs stretched out. She is made of dark lines and circles on a brown background. Little stick figures are around her. The picture looks playful, like a child's drawing, but Klee planned it carefully. How would you dance with her?
descriptions.g35: Paul Klee, a German-Swiss artist, painted Dancing Girl in 1940. A pink, simplified figure dances with outstretched limbs, drawn in dark lines and circles on a brown ground, with small figures around her. Klee made many pictures like this near the end of his life. How does he show movement with simple lines? What makes it feel playful?
descriptions.g68: Klee painted Dancing Girl in 1940, the year he died. After the Nazis came to power, he lost his teaching job in 1933 and went into exile in Switzerland; from 1937 to 1940 his output surged again. The museum notes his humor, including a signature made by laying a handkerchief on the surface. How do simple lines and playful figures show energy, and what might the humor mean in hard times?
descriptions.g910: Dancing Girl (1940) comes from the last years of Klee's life, when, after losing his teaching post in 1933 and leaving Germany, he again produced many paintings and drawings. Its pink, abstracted dancer, drawn in dark lines and circles with small figures around her, combines childlike simplicity with deliberate design. The museum notes his humor. Consider how playfulness and seriousness coexist, and what a dance can suggest in a period of exile.
descriptions.g1112: Painted in Klee's final year, Dancing Girl exemplifies the late style of bold, calligraphic line and simplified figures. The museum places it within a surge of productivity from 1937 to 1940 following his dismissal from teaching in 1933 and exile in Switzerland, and notes his humor, including a monogrammed handkerchief used to make the signature. How does the work balance childlike spontaneity with sophisticated control, and how far should biography shape our reading of its tone?

teacherNote.context: A 1940 oil painting by Paul Klee in the Art Institute of Chicago, showing a simplified dancing figure drawn in dark lines. The museum places it in Klee's late burst of productivity after exile and notes his humor. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students draw a dancing figure in one continuous line, then add small color accents.
Ask students to list ways Klee suggests movement without realistic detail.
Discuss how humor and playfulness appear in serious times.
